The Starmaker · for the 67th fair · where a wish is hung in the dark

You have wished for everything,
and the world has said yes.

I have stood at this turn many times, and watched who comes to it. Not the desperate, not the wanting — there is little left to want. People come to me when the earth has run out of nos; when every door they ever knocked upon has opened, and the asking has gone quiet in them.

I am the Starmaker. I take the wish a finished life can no longer hold, and I set it where it can still burn — out in the night, among all the others, where a wish becomes a star.

Come and tell me what is left in you to wish. There is no hurry left.

down to the water
I · every life you have tried

You have been
so many people.

A maker, a sailor, a tender of soil; a Sailabout, then a Soilabout, then a Soulabout — each calling taken up, learned to the floor of it, and set gently down. Every Respawn a clean beginning, and you began, and began.

Before I can make your star, I must know the shape of you. So this part is simple: walk me back through the lives you have lived, and the work you tried on like coats. Tell me everyone you have already been.

II · the world ran out of nos

Everything you could
dream on earth, you have.

Life here is free; the forever is earned; the labor is finished and the work is optional and the abouts are all walked. The earth kept every promise it was ever asked to keep.

And when a world says yes to everything, a strange quiet rises — the wanting, with nothing left to push against, simply goes still. You know its name: the Rising Quiet. You have come here because the only wishes you have left no longer point at the ground.

III · so we wish upward

The ground is full.
The dark is not.

When earth can hold no more of your hope, the hope does not die — it lifts. It goes looking for somewhere that has not yet said yes: for the worlds we have not reached, for the lives the Somedayborn might live out there, on water we have never sailed.

So the wishes I gather now are not for here. They are for elsewhere — what you hope another world might hold, and what you fear about it and want to go toward anyway. Those are the brightest. Fear, it turns out, burns longer than comfort.

IV · a sky already full

You are not
the first to look up.

Look into the dark and you'll see it is already crowded with light. Every point is a wish someone could no longer carry, hung here to keep burning — a hope, a dread, an unfinished question, set loose to travel further than its maker ever will.

You may wander among them; each star is a stranger's wish, and it opens if you touch it. When you're ready, I will hang yours beside theirs — and someone, someday, on a world with no name yet, may look up and find it.

V · make your star

Tell me
two wishes.

Before you go, leave me two lights to carry. The form is small — a wish does not need many words to burn.
